clinicalPearls: A form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, most often caused by variants in TGM1 encoding transglutaminase-1, with several other causative genes
Typically presents at birth as a collodion baby encased in a taut, shiny membrane that sheds over the first weeks
Evolves into large, plate-like, dark brown adherent scales with relatively little underlying erythema, contrasting with the erythrodermic phenotype
Ectropion and eclabium are common and cause chronic ocular exposure problems
Scalp scarring alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, and reduced sweating with heat intolerance are frequent
Sits on a clinical spectrum with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma; some patients show overlapping features
Management centres on topical emollients and keratolytics, with oral retinoids for severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Lamellar ichthyosis most commonly arises from deficiency of transglutaminase-1, an enzyme that cross-links structural proteins to form the cornified cell envelope and covalently attaches lipids to the envelope surface. Loss of enzyme activity prevents formation of a normal cornified envelope and disrupts the lipid scaffold of the stratum corneum, impairing the permeability barrier and desquamation. Compensatory hyperproliferation and retention of corneocytes produce the characteristic thick, plate-like scaling. Other causative genes (including those for lipid transport and processing) can produce overlapping phenotypes within the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis spectrum.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing including TGM1 and other congenital ichthyosis genes
Skin biopsy showing marked orthohyperkeratosis with a normal or thickened granular layer
In vitro transglutaminase-1 activity assay where available
Ophthalmology assessment for ectropion and corneal exposure
Assessment of thermoregulation and hydration, particularly in neonates
Prenatal or carrier genetic testing for at-risk families
redFlags: Neonatal dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and temperature instability in the collodion phase
Corneal exposure and ulceration from severe ectropion
Heat intolerance and hyperthermia from impaired sweating
Secondary skin infection of fissured skin
reference.prognosis: It is a lifelong disorder; after the vulnerable collodion period most patients stabilise into chronic generalised scaling that requires continuous skin care, with visual and thermoregulatory complications influencing overall morbidity.
pitfalls: Assuming all collodion babies have lamellar ichthyosis when the membrane can precede several distinct disorders
Overlooking heat intolerance from anhidrosis, risking hyperthermia in warm environments or exercise
Neglecting ophthalmic monitoring for ectropion-related corneal damage
Failing to counsel on the recessive inheritance and recurrence risk
management: Base daily care on liberal emollients and keratolytics such as urea and alpha-hydroxy acids to soften and reduce the plate-like scale
In the collodion neonate, nurse in a humidified incubator with careful fluid and electrolyte balance, emollients and monitoring for sepsis and thermoregulatory instability
Consider systemic retinoids such as acitretin for severe, disabling scaling
Provide ophthalmology care for ectropion and corneal exposure with lubrication and surgical correction where needed
Manage heat intolerance from impaired sweating and remain vigilant for skin and systemic infection
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across dermatology, ophthalmology and ENT with psychological support
Offer genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing for at-risk families given autosomal recessive inheritance
